COURT-1
IN THE APPELLATE TRIBUNAL FOR ELECTRICITY
(Appellate Jurisdiction)
IA No. 1939 of 2026
in
Appeal No. 196 OF 2026
Dated : 23rd September, 2026
Present: Hon`ble Ms. Seema Gupta, Officiating Chairperson
Hon`ble Mr. Virender Bhat, Judicial Member
In the matter of:
PSEB Engineers Association .... Appellant(s)
Versus
Punjab State Electricity Regulatory Commission & Ors. .... Respondent(s)
Counsel on record for the Appellant(s) : Anushree Bardhan
Srishti Khindaria
Ritika Singh
Somya Sahni
Rashmi Vaish for App. 1
Counsel on record for the : Gargi Kumar for Res. 1
Respondent(s)
Anand K. Ganesan
Swapna Seshadri
Amal Nair
Devyani Prasad for Res. 2
Aditya Grover
Arjun Grover
Pooja Sharma for Res. 3
ORDER
IA-1939/2026
(For impleadment/ intervention)
1. The applicant namely Department of Power, Govt. of Punjab is
seeking impleadment as a party to this appeal in which the tariff order
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 1 of 15

dated 06.03.2026 issued by 1st Respondent – Punjab Electricity
Regulatory Commission (in short “the Commission”) in petition No. 70 of
2025 filed by 2nd Respondent – Punjab State Power Corporation Ltd. (in
short PSPCL) for true-up of Aggregate Revenue Requirement (ARR) for
Financial Year 2024-25, approval of forecast of ARR for 4th MYT control
period from Financial Year 2026-27 to Financial Year 2028-29 and
determination of Tariff for Financial Year 2026-27. Vide the impugned
order, the Commission has, inter alia :-
“(i) Approved a Distribution Loss Trajectory of 10.00% for FY
2026-27, 9.95% for FY 2027-28, and 9.90% for FY 2028-29;
(ii) Approved a Net Revenue Requirement of Rs. 48,996 Cr for
FY 2026-27;
(iii) Treated loss funding of Rs. 3,581.95 Cr received by PSPCL
from the Government of Punjab during FY 2024-25 as Non-Tariff
Income under Regulation 27 of the PSERC MYT Regulations,
2022;
(iv) Computed a revenue surplus of Rs. 7,851.91 Cr for FY
2026-27; and
(v) Reduced the Government subsidy obligation to Rs. 15,200
Cr from the projected Rs. 22,250 Cr.”
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 2 of 15

2. Apart from seeking impleadment in this appeal, the applicant has
also sought permission to file reply to the memorandum of appeal and to
address all issues having a direct or consequential bearing upon subsidy
and Government funding.
3. We have heard Mr. Buddy Ranganadhan, Learned Senior Counsel
and Mr. Vivek Jain, Additional Advocate General appearing on behalf of
the applicant and Mr. Sitesh Mukherjee, Learned Senior Counsel
appearing on behalf of the Appellant. Written submissions filed on behalf
of the parties have also been perused.
4. According to Learned Senior Counsel for the applicant, the contents
of paragraphs I, J & K at page 14 and paragraphs U & V at page 18 of the
memorandum of appeal have given rise to a genuine cause and occasion
for the applicant to seek impleadment in this appeal. For the sake of
convenience, we extract these paragraphs of the memorandum of appeal
hereunder :-
“I. BECAUSE the State Commission has, in para 2.31 of the
Impugned Order, treated the loss funding of Rs. 3,581.95 Cr
received by PSPCL from the Government of Punjab during FY
2024-25 as Non-Tariff Income under Regulation 27 of the PSERC
MYT Regulations, 2022. This is erroneous.
J. BECAUSE the State Commission failed to consider that
PSPCL itself had expressly submitted in the original ARR petition
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 3 of 15

(para 2.24.3, page 54) that the said amount has NOT been treated
as Non-Tariff Income stating "It is pertinent to mention here that
during FY 2024-25, PSPCL, has received grant in the form of loss
funding from the government of Punjab to the tune of Rs. 3582 Cr.
The same has however not been treated as part of non-tariff
income in accordance with earlier approach towards similar loss
funding under UDAY scheme, which was also followed by the
Hon'ble Commission".
However, in complete volta face, in the revised submissions, para
8, page 4, PSPCL submitted, "Further, in continuation of this office
memo No. 826/Arr/DY.CAO/271/Deficiencies dated 17.12.2026, it
is submitted that during FY 2024-25, PSPCL received loss funding
amounting to Rs. 3581.95 Reform the Government of Punjab. The
said funding was extended as a prerequisite for enabling the
Government of Punjab to avail additional borrowing equivalent to
0.5% of GSDP from Government of India. The accounting
treatment & presentation of the aforesaid grant in the financial
statements of the companies have been carried out in accordance
with applicable Ind AS and schedule III of companies Act 2013.
However, the treatment of the same in tariff petition may be
considered in accordance with Regulation 27 of PSERC MYT
Regulations, 2022."
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 4 of 15

K. BECAUSE the State Commission failed to appreciate that
the Government of Punjab extended this funding as a prerequisite
for availing additional borrowing equivalent to 0.5% of GSDP from
the Government of India, It is a capital grant for operational
rehabilitation, not operational income. The purpose of loss funding
is to compensate PSPCL for accumulated losses and to improve
its financial position. Treating it as Non-Tariff Income would
negate this purpose entirely and PSPCL would effectively be
paying back through a reduced ARR what was given to it as a
financial support………………………………………………………
…………………………………………………………………………..
U. BECAUSE the facts on record make it abundantly clear that
the impugned Order was passed in undue haste to enable the
Government of Punjab to present its State Budget before the
Punjab Legislative Assembly on 08.03.2026, with the reduced
tariff and substantially reduced Government subsidy obligation
incorporated therein.
V. BECAUSE FY 2026-27 is an election year for the Punjab
State Legislative Assembly. It is a pattern evident from year-wise
data that in election years, the State has consistently resorted to
reduction or nil increase in tariff, followed by tariff shock for
consumers in subsequent years. The Impugned Order follows this
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 5 of 15

very pattern and is being passed not in the consumer interest or
in the interest of the financially sustainable functioning of PSPCL,
but in the political interest of the ruling party, thereby defeating the
very purpose of independent economic regulation under the
Electricity Act, 2003.”
5. It is submitted by the Learned Senior Counsel that the contents of
paragraphs U & V are direct imputations against the State Government of
Punjab and the Government has a natural right to respond to the same.
He would further submit that the contents of paragraphs I, J & K deal with
the nature of grant given by the Government and, therefore, it can hardly
be said that the Govt. is not a necessary party to the appeal as the nature
of grant given by it, is the core and central issue.
6. The Learned Senior Counsel further argued that the State
Government is necessary party to this appeal and has a right to be heard
as :-
(a) The tariff order is binding on the State Government (see
judgement dated 26.05.2026 of this Tribunal in Appeal Nos. 4
of 2005 and batch SIEL vs. PSERC) and hence, the State
Govt. has right to be heard before it is passed as well as in the
appeal against it;
(b) Apart from being itself a consumer as its offices also pay
electricity tariff and thus entitled to be heard in a tariff appeal,
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 6 of 15

the State Government is the “Parens Patraie” of the
consumers in the State and therefore, dutybound to protect
their interests;
(c) The State Governments’ bill depends upon the tariff which is
determined by the Regulator and/or in the appeal by this
Tribunal, it has a right to be heard before such determination;
and
(d) State budget for Financial Year 2026-27 has been laid before
the Punjab Legislative Assembly on the determined figure of
subsidy and a mid-year alteration of the tariff would require
supplementary provision, thereby disturbing commitments
already made across the budget and would unsettle the fiscal
stance of the entire state.
7. Reliance is placed upon the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court
in A.P. Transco Vs. Sai Renewable Power (P) Ltd. (2011) 11 SCC 34
wherein the apex court wondered why this Tribunal did not implead the
State as a party to the appeal proceedings when the Tribunal, in its
judgement, had referred to various acts & deeds of the State as well as
the consequences thereof.
8. On these submissions, the Learned Senior Counsel Mr. Buddy
Ranganadhan urged us to implead the applicant as a respondent to this
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 7 of 15

appeal and to permit it to file its response and to address arguments on
the above noted issues raised in the appeal.
9. The application is vehemently resisted on behalf of the Appellant.
Mr. Mukherjee, Learned Senior Counsel for the Appellant argued that the
applicant i.e. State of Punjab is neither a proper nor a necessary party to
this appeal as neither has any relief been sought against it nor is any of
its order/decision/policy under challenge. He would submit that upon
enactment of Electricity Act, 2003, the power to fix tariff is vested with the
State Electricity Regulatory Commissions and the State Governments
have no role in that exercise. Referring to Section 108 of the Electricity
Act, he submitted that the State Govt. has not been given any say in the
tariff fixation even while exercising power under this provision of the
statute. He argued that no provision in the Electricity Act confers
jurisdiction upon this Tribunal either to pass orders for or against the State
Government and this Tribunal does not exercise any jurisdiction over the
State Government. On this aspect, he cited the judgement of this Tribunal
dated 17.01.2025 in Execution Petition No. 12/2023 titled Ratnagiri Gas
and Power Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Maharashtra State Electricity Distribution Co. Ltd.
10. According to the Learned Senior Counsel, the judgement in
Transmission Co. of Andhra Pradesh (supra) and SIEL Ltd. (supra) has
been rendered in altogether distinct factual aspects of that case and is not
applicable to the instant case.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 8 of 15

11. Thus, on these submissions, the dismissal of the application is
sought.
12. We may note that the proceedings in a tariff petition before the
Commission are of inquisitorial in nature and not adversarial, as there is
no respondent or opposite party in the petition. By way of such a petition,
a generator or a distribution licensee or a transmission licensee, as the
case may be, seeks approval of its ARR and determination of tariff for the
power generated and/or supplied or transmitted by using the assets of the
entity. The usual course adopted by the regulatory commissions for such
petition is to issue a public notice in the newspapers having circulation in
the concerned State inviting objections/comments from the stakeholders
as well as the general public. The Commission also holds public hearings
on such objections/comments received from the general public and the
stakeholders. Thereafter, upon analyzing the contentions of the petitioner
and upon considering the objections/comments of the general public and
stakeholders, the tariff order is passed by the Commission.
13. In the instant case also, the Commission has followed the said
course before issuing the impugned tariff order, which is evident from a
bare reading of the order particularly paragraph Nos. 1.4, 1.5, 1.7 and 1.9.
Perusal of the order reveals that the State Govt. of Punjab did not submit
any objections or comments in response to the public notice issued on the
petition of 2nd Respondent. Accordingly, the Commission addressed two
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 9 of 15

D.O. letters dated 08.01.2026 and 23.01.2026 to the State Government
seeking its views on the petition but these did not evoke any response
from the Govt. Ultimately, the Commission was constrained to issue
another D.O. letter dated 08.02.2026 to the State Govt. with the request
to convey its decision in respect of subsidies in various categories of the
consumers for Financial Year 2026-27, which was then conveyed by the
State Govt. vide memo dated 04.03.2026. The contents of the said memo
have been taken note of in paragraph 6.4 at page 232 of the impugned
tariff order and have been considered for arriving at the amount of subsidy
to be released by the State Govt. to the 2nd Respondent – PSPCL.
14. We have already extracted the paragraph Nos. I, J, K, U & V of the
memorandum of appeal hereinabove, which according to the applicant
relate to it and need its response. The paragraphs I, J & K relate the
treatment to the funding received by 2nd Respondent – PSPCL from the
State Govt. The Commission, in the impugned order, had permitted the
PSPCL to treat the loss funding by the State Government as non-tariff
income, which, according to the Appellant is erroneous and contrary to the
purpose of loss funding. The contents of the paragraphs U and V are in
the nature of direct allegations against the State Govt.
15. Undisputedly, there is no provision in the Electricity Act that confers
jurisdiction upon this Tribunal to pass orders either in favour of or against
a State Government, as rightly observed in Ratnagiri Case (supra). This
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 10 of 15

Tribunal does not exercise any jurisdiction over the State Government.
The power to examine the orders passed by the State Regulatory
Commissions has been conferred upon this Tribunal under Section 111 of
the Electricity Act, 2003, which is quoted hereunder :-
“Section 111. (Appeal to Appellate Tribunal): --- (1) Any
person aggrieved by an order made by an adjudicating
officer under this Act (except under section 127) or an order
made by the Appropriate Commission under this Act may
prefer an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity:
Provided that any person appealing against the order of the
adjudicating officer levying any penalty shall, while filing the
appeal , deposit the amount of such penalty:
Provided further that wherein any particular case, the
Appellate Tribunal is of the opinion that the deposit of such
penalty would cause undue hardship to such person, it may
dispense with such deposit subject to such conditions as it
may deem fit to impose so as to safeguard the realisation
of penalty.
(2) Every appeal under sub-section (1) shall be filed within
a period of forty- five days from the date on which a copy of
the order made by the adjudicating officer or the
Appropriate Commission is received by the aggrieved
person and it shall be in such form, verified in such manner
and be accompanied by such fee as may be prescribed:
Provided that the Appellate Tribunal may entertain an
appeal after the expiry of the said period of forty-five days if
it is satisfied that there was sufficient cause for not filing it
within that period.
(3) On receipt of an appeal under sub-section (1), the
Appellate Tribunal may, after giving the parties to the appeal
an opportunity of being heard, pass such orders thereon as
it thinks fit, confirming, modifying or setting aside the order
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 11 of 15

appealed against.
(4) The Appellate Tribunal shall send a copy of every order
made by it to the parties to the appeal and to the concerned
adjudicating officer or the Appropriate Commission, as the
case may be.
(5) The appeal filed before the Appellate Tribunal under
sub-section (1) shall be dealt with by it as expeditiously as
possible and endeavour shall be made by it to dispose of the
appeal finally within one hundred and eighty days from the
date of receipt of the appeal:
Provided that where any appeal could not be disposed of
within the said period of one hundred and eighty days, the
Appellate Tribunal shall record its reasons in writing for not
disposing of the appeal within the said period.
(6) The Appellate Tribunal may, for the purpose of
examining the legality, propriety or correctness of any order
made by the adjudicating officer or the Appropriate
Commission under this Act, as the case may be, in relation
to any proceeding, on its own motion or otherwise, call for
the records of such proceedings and make such order in
the case as it thinks fit.
16. Perusal of this statutory provision reveals that any person, who feels
aggrieved by any order passed by a State Electricity Regulatory
Commission, can file an appeal against that order in this Tribunal. Thus
the party aggrieved would be the Appellant and the party in whose favour
the order has been passed would be the respondent other than the
Commission itself, to resist the appeal.
17. The order impugned in this appeal is the tariff order passed by the
Commission in the tariff petition filed by the 2nd Respondent – PSPCL.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 12 of 15

18. However, there might arise situations where some
explanation/comments are sought from the State Government by the
Regulatory Commission before passing the tariff order or some
observations are made regarding any action of the State Government in
the tariff order, which are subsequently highlighted in the appeal before
this Tribunal against the tariff order and made a ground to assail the order.
In such an appeal, this Tribunal would be constrained to analyze the
actions of the State Govt. and consider the stand taken by the State Govt.
before the Commission. Therefore, in those circumstances, it would not
be appropriate for this Tribunal to comment adversely upon the actions of
the State Govt. or the stand it had taken before the Commission on any
issue, without affording an opportunity of hearing to the State Govt.
19. Even though the facts of the case before the Hon’ble Supreme Court
in A.P. Transco Case (supra) may not be identical to the facts of this case
yet the dictum of that case that this Tribunal could not have referred to the
acts and deeds of the State as well as consequences thereof without
impleading the State as a party to the appeal, is squarely applicable to the
instant case.
20. In the instant appeal, one of the grounds of challenge to the
impugned order of the Commission is the treatment given to the loss
funding of the Govt. based upon the comments of the State Govt. The
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 13 of 15

Appellant had also commented adversely upon the acts of the State Govt.
in paragraphs U & V of the memorandum of appeal.
21. Considering the fact that the findings of the Commission in the
impugned order with regards to the treatment to the loss funding of the
State Govt. are based upon the contents of memo dated 04.03.2026 of
the State Govt. and also taking note of the statements concerning the
State Govt. in paragraphs U & V of the memorandum of appeal, we are of
the considered opinion that the State Govt. must be afforded opportunity
to file its response limited to these five paragraphs in the memorandum of
appeal which would assist us in arriving at a just decision on the aspect of
nature and treatment of loss fundings/subsidy granted by it. Taking a
contrary view would be against the settled principles of justice, equity and
fairplay.
22. Hence, we allow the application and implead the Department of
Power, State Govt. of Punjab as Respondent No. 4 in this appeal.
However, we make it clear that the State Govt. has been impleaded for
the limited purpose of responding to contents of paragraph No. I, J, K, U
& V in the memorandum of appeal and hence, its reply as well as the
submissions shall be confined to the averments contained in these five
paragraphs in the impugned order.
Appeal No. 196 of 2026
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I.A. No. 1939 of 2026 Page 14 of 15

23. The Appellant shall file amended memo of parties within one week
from today.
24. The Department of Power, Govt. of Punjab shall file its reply within
two weeks from today to which the Appellant shall file rejoinder within one
week thereafter.
I.A. Nos. 732 & 1819 of 2026
25. List for hearing on 21.10.2026.
Pronounced in the open court on this 23rd day of September, 2026.
Virender Bhat Seema Gupta
Judicial Member Officiating Chairperson

JUDGMENT
PER HON’BLE MR. VIRENDER BHAT, JUDICIAL MEMBER
The Appellant, a distribution licensee in the State of Gujarat, has
filed this Appeal against the Tariff Order dated 04.04.2018 passed by the
Gujarat Electricity Regulatory Commission (hereinafter referred to as the
APL No. 171 OF 2018 Page 2 of 5

“State Commission/Commission”) with regards to the true up for the FY
2016-17 and determination of tariff for FY 2018-19.
The only ground of challenge to the impugned order of the
Commission raised in this Appeal is with regards to the methodology
adopted by the Commission in respect of the treatment given to
Operation and Maintenance (O&M) Expenses of the Appellant. The
Commission, in the impugned order, has treated the O&M Expenses as
controllable. According to the Appellant, the impugned order on this
aspect is contrary to law as well as the applicable regulations and
therefore, cannot be sustained.
We have heard the Learned Counsels for the parties and perused
the written submissions filed by them.
Both, the Appellant and as well as the Respondent No.1-
Commission have stated in its written submissions that the instant case
is squarely covered by the judgment of this Tribunal dated 09.05.2019 in
Appeal No. 256 of 2016 titled “Torrent Power Limited Vs. Gujarat
Electricity Regulatory Commission wherein it has been held as under: -
“9.1 The variation in O&M expense is normally to be treated as
controllable. However, in exception cases as in hand, the
amount of Network Augmentation charges incurred by the
Appellant as required by State Transmission Utility (STU) for
connectivity needs to be treated as uncontrollable.
APL No. 171 OF 2018 Page 3 of 5

9.2 The deduction of Rs. 2.48 crores from O & M Expenses are
contrary to applicable Statutory Regulations of the State
Commission.
9.3 The Commission should take consistent stand in all matters
on the same plea whether related to O&M expenses or the
variation in technical and commercial losses.”
The State Commission, in its written submission, has further stated
that the Commission is bound by the directions passed by this Tribunal
in the above noted judgment and has prayed that the matter may be
remanded back to the Commission for a fresh decision in terms of the
said judgment of this Tribunal.
In view of such admitted legal position enunciated by this Tribunal
in Appeal 256 judgment (supra) and considering the consensus between
the parties with regards to the applicability of the said judgment to this
case, we consider it appropriate not to go into the merits of the case and
instead remand the case back to the Commission for a fresh decision in
terms of the said judgment.
Accordingly, we hereby set aside the impugned order, allow the
Appeal and remand the case back to the Commission for a fresh decision
with regards to the treatment to be given to O&M charges in terms of the
judgment of this Tribunal dated 09.05.2019 in Appeal No. 256 of 2016
APL No. 171 OF 2018 Page 4 of 5

titled “Torrent Power Limited Vs. Gujarat Electricity Regulatory
Commission.
The Appeal and the IA therein stand disposed of accordingly.
Pronounced in the open court on this 22nd day of September,
2026.
Ajay Talegaonkar Virender Bhat
Technical Member (Electricity) Judicial Member

J U D G M E N T
PER HON’BLE MR. AJAY TALEGAONKAR, TECHNICAL MEMBER
Background and Factual Matrix
1. The Appellant i.e. Serum Institute of India Private Limited (“SIIPL”) is
engaged in the business of manufacturing immuno-biological drugs
including vaccines in India. The Appellant is also a generating company
within the meaning of Section 2(28) of the Electricity Act, 2003 and has set
up Wind Energy Power Plants having total installed capacity of 57.2 MW in
District- Dhule, Sangli and Satara in the State of Maharashtra. The present
appeal is filed by M/s Serum Institute of India Private Limited
(“Appellant/SIIPL”) challenging the Impugned Order dated 30.05.2019
passed by Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (“Respondent
No. 1”/ “MERC”) in Case No. 49 of 2019.
Page 2 of 16

Judgement in Appeal No.294 of 2019
2. The SIIPL had established wind generating capacity of 56.5 MW at 3
locations after Government of Maharashtra (“GoM”) introduced New Policy
for Power Generation from Non-Conventional Sources of Energy, 2008
(“GOM Policy, 2008”). This capacity is identified as falling under Group-IV.
Prior to this, after enactment of the Electricity Act, 2003 also, SIIPL had
established 0.7 MW capacity, which identified as falling under Group-II.
3. The Appellant utilised the generation primarily for captive/ self-use
and also supplied part of the energy to third-party consumers through Open
Access (“OA”). During FY 2014-15 and FY 2015-16, where third-party
consumers were not available for the entire generation, the Appellant
obtained MSEDCL’s permission to sell surplus wind energy to MSEDCL on
a short-term basis at the applicable tariff.
4. During FY 2017-18, the Appellant’s consumers applied for Short-
Term Open Access (“STOA”). The Appellant states that, as a result, its
captive utilisation and third-party OA sales were restricted, leaving surplus
wind energy for which eligible OA consumers were not available. The
MERC (Distribution Open Access) Regulations, 2016 (“DOA Regulations,
2016”) came into effect in April 2016, replacing the 2014 Regulations and,
inter alia, restoring banking provisions applicable to RE.
5. Between April 2016 and March 2018, the Appellant generated and
injected 3,67,58,630 units of wind energy into the MSEDCL grid. For FY

Our Analysis and Conclusions
17. We have heard the Learned Counsel for the Appellant and the
Learned Counsel for the Respondent at length. We have also carefully
considered their respective submissions and the relevant material on
record. Upon due consideration of the arguments advanced and the
documents placed before us; we now proceed to analyse the issues arising
for our consideration in the present Appeal.
18. We note that the Appellant has primarily based its case on Section
70 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872. On the other hand, MSEDCL has
supported the Impugned Order primarily on the basis of the DOA
Regulations, 2016 and the requirement of maintenance of grid discipline,
while at the same time refuting the applicability of Section 70 of the Indian
Contract Act.
19. We note that Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act is premised on the
absence of a contract governing the transaction. A contract may be an
express or implied agreement between the parties regarding the exchange
of goods/ services and the consideration thereof, roles and responsibilities
of the parties, timelines, dispute resolution, etc. In the power sector,
however, many of the terms and conditions governing transactions are
prescribed by the Regulations framed by the Central Commission or the
State Commissions, as the case may. Such Regulations are binding and
may either supplement the terms and conditions of contracts or, where any
provision of a contract is contrary to the applicable Regulations, prevail over
such contractual provisions (PTC India Ltd. v. CERC, 2010 4 SCC 603).
Page 7 of 16

Judgement in Appeal No.294 of 2019
20. In view of the above, we are of the opinion that, in the power sector,
while examining the applicability of Section 70 of the Indian Contract Act, it
is necessary to consider not only whether there is a contract governing the
transaction, but also whether the transaction is governed by any binding
Regulation. Where the transaction is governed by Regulations, the rights
and obligations of the parties have to be determined within the framework
thereof before recourse can be taken to Section 70 of the Indian Contract
Act.
21. In view of the forgoing, we would like to closely examine the
provisions of DOA Regulations, 2016 and their relevance in the present
controversy. MSEDCL in their submissions have referred to Regulation
5.10.5 and 8.10 of the DOA Regulations, 2016. We also observe that in the
para 12.2 of the Impugned Order, a provision of DOA Regulations, 2016
regarding a limit of 10% of excess injection has been mentioned. A perusal
of DOA Regulations, 2016 reveals such provision can be found in
Regulation 20. In fact, Appellant has also referred to Regulation 20.6
regarding deemed purchase of excess energy injection. In order to analyse

22. We find that the reliance placed by MSEDCL on Regulation 5.10.5 is
misplaced. It can be seen that this Regulation forms part of Regulation 5.10,
which deals with the treatment of infirm power. Regulation 5.10.1 clearly
indicates that infirm power is the power generated during testing prior to the
commercial operation or grant of open access of the generating station.
When viewed in this context, it is clear that Regulation 5.10.5 only prohibits
injection of infirm power without a proper agreement with the distribution
licensee. In the case at hand, the wind generating stations were already
under commercial operation and had been granted open access for a long
time. Therefore, categorising the excess energy injected by the Appellant
as infirm power is clearly incorrect.
23. Another Regulation relied upon by MSEDCL, namely Regulation
8.10, also deals with the situation prior to the grant of open access and, in
effect, provides that open access shall be granted only if the resulting flow
Page 12 of 16

Judgement in Appeal No.294 of 2019
can be accommodated. In the present case, open access had already been
granted and was operational, but the energy injected was in excess of the
permitted limit. We shall examine the consequences of such excess
injection separately. However, Regulation 8.10 cannot be construed as a
provision prohibiting excess injection after open access has already been
granted.
24. On the other hand, Regulation 20 has definite applicability in the
present case. Sub-Regulation 20.2 categorically provides that any excess
injection from renewable generators shall be banked with the distribution
licensee. The subsequent sub-Regulations of Regulation 20 deal in detail
with the accounting of such banked energy, and sub-Regulation 20.6
specifically provides that unutilised banked energy at the end of the
financial year, limited to 10% of the actual total generation by such
Renewable Energy generator during such financial year, shall be
considered as deemed purchase by the Distribution Licensee at its Pooled
Cost of Power Purchase for that year. Therefore, in our opinion, MSEDCL
was bound to treat the appropriate quantum of excess energy injected as
deemed purchase in accordance with Regulation 20.6. MERC has, though,
referred to this provision in the Impugned Order, but failed to direct
MSEDCL to implement the same.
25. We do not find the contention of MSEDCL, or the finding of MERC
with regard to maintenance of grid discipline to be appropriate. While there
is no doubt that grid discipline is of utmost importance, the distribution
licensee and/ or SLDC are fully empowered under the Grid Code to issue
specific instructions for reduction of generation in the event of a
Page 13 of 16

Judgement in Appeal No.294 of 2019
contingency, even where such injection is well within the contracted
capacity. Regulation 29 of the DOA Regulations, 2016 also clearly provides
for curtailment of a transaction during operation, subject to the provisions
of the Grid Code. However, there is nothing on record to show that the
excess energy injected by the Appellant’s generating plants over and above
the contracted capacity was in violation of any specific instruction to restrict
injection for maintaining grid security. Further, we note that the two orders
referred to in the Impugned Order, namely, (i) MERC Order in Case No. 86
of 2016 and (ii) MERC Order in Case No. 120 of 2018, are dated
11.04.2018 and 25.07.2018, respectively, and were issued after the lapse
of the period in controversy, i.e., 01.04.2016 to 31.03.2018. Therefore,
MSEDCL and MERC obviously cannot rely upon any direction contained in
those orders. Further, these orders were related to injection by a generator
without any agreement, which is not the situation in the present case.
26. Most importantly, when the field was governed by Regulations having
the force of law, an order cannot be relied upon to circumvent or override
the provisions of such Regulations.
27. We note that the Appellants have relied upon the object of the Act to
promote renewable energy and the MUST RUN status under the MERC
(Terms & Conditions for Determination of Renewable Energy Tariff)
Regulations, 2015 while seeking deemed sale to MSEDCL of the entire
excess energy injected by their generating stations. To us, it appears that
the provision for banking of energy and deemed purchase thereof, as it was
prevailing then, was itself a promotional measure. However, where the
Page 14 of 16

Judgement in Appeal No.294 of 2019
applicable Regulations specifically provide for the treatment of excess
energy, such promotional measure cannot be extended beyond the
treatment specifically prescribed therein. Further, since the Appellants were
using open access for drawing power for their captive use and for third-
party sale, the applicable regulatory framework is the DOA Regulations,
2016.
28. In view of the specific provision under the DOA Regulations, 2016,
which came into effect from 01.04.2016, governing the treatment of excess
energy, we do not consider it necessary to take into account the past
practice of post facto approval by MSEDCL of sale of excess energy, as
pointed out by the Appellant. For the same reason, neither the absence of
consent nor the question whether MSEDCL was aware of the excess
injection alters the applicability of the said regulatory provision and is,
therefore, not material to the controversy.
29. Since we have concluded, for the reasons already elaborated, that
the DOA Regulations, 2016 are applicable for the treatment of excess
energy injected by the Appellants’ generating stations, we do not find it
necessary to examine the aspect of undue enrichment under Section 70 of
the Indian Contract Act.
ORDER
For the foregoing reasons as stated above, the captioned Appeal No. 294
of 2019 is allowed and the Impugned Order is set aside to the extent it
disallows deemed purchase of entire excess energy injected by the wind
generating stations of the Appellant.
